intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself against the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: Who farms, and on how much land
sections.big_idea: Three surveys count three different things, and most Indian holdings are **under one hectare**. Know the unit before you quote a number.
in_plain_words: The Agriculture Census counts holdings, the Situation Assessment Survey counts agricultural households and the labour force survey counts workers. A holding run by two brothers is one holding and two households, so the totals differ without any of them being wrong.

Once the unit is clear, the land picture is stark. Marginal holdings are 68.45 per cent of all holdings and operate 24.03 per cent of the land. **The average holding fell because more holdings slid into the small class**, while each class kept roughly its own size.

children.label: Agriculture Census
items: By size, social group and sex of holder

diagram.caption: ask for the survey, the year and the unit

key_terms.meaning: All land managed as one unit by a household, whatever the title.
Land held with permanent heritable possession.
A holding below one hectare.
A household with produce worth over ₹4,000 a year and a self-employed farming member.
The monsoon season and the winter season.
One lakh is 100,000; one crore is 10 million.

worked_example.title: How small is the typical holding?
worked_example.setup: Use the 2015-16 Agriculture Census figures from the deck.
steps: Marginal holdings: 100.25 ÷ 146.45 = 68.45% of all holdings.
Add the small class: 68.45 + 17.62 = 86.07% of holdings are under two hectares.
Average size: 157.82 ÷ 146.45 = 1.08 hectares.
Compare 1.08 with the marginal class average of 0.38 hectares.
worked_example.answer: About 86% of holdings are under two hectares, so the typical holder farms well under the 1.08 hectare average.

mistakes: Comparing a holdings count from the census with a households count from the survey as if they measured the same thing.
Designing a scheme for the average farmer, who operates a farm that very few people actually run.
Reading the falling average holding as farms shrinking inside every size class.

recall.q: Which source counts operational holdings?
recall.a: The Agriculture Census, latest published for 2015-16.

recall.q: What share of holdings are marginal, and how much land do they hold?
recall.a: 68.45 per cent of holdings on 24.03 per cent of the area.

recall.q: What is the difference between owning and operating land?
recall.a: A tenant operates land and owns none. Schemes that pay owners and schemes that pay operators reach different people.

recall.q: Why does the NSS count of holdings (101.98 million) sit below the census (146.45 million)?
recall.a: The NSS counts rural households, and multiple holdings within one household are not distinguished. The census counts every holding.

recall.q: Who is outside the Situation Assessment Survey by definition?
recall.a: Households that live entirely on farm labour.

sections.title: Incomes and indebtedness
sections.big_idea: Farm income depends on **which costs you deduct**, and wages now earn farm households more than crops do.
in_plain_words: The 2019 survey builds household income from five lines and reports it twice. Deducting only cash costs gives ₹10,218 a month. Also deducting the value of family labour, own seed and own land gives ₹8,337. Neither is wrong, and they answer different questions.

Around that sit a few habits. Say whether a figure is nominal or real, prefer medians to means, and convert household figures to per person. **A debt total hides the interest rate, the lender and the purpose**, so it tells you little about distress by itself.

diagram.note: two totals: ₹10,218 with cash costs deducted, ₹8,337 with imputed costs too

key_terms.meaning: Receipts less expenses for that activity.
Cash the household actually spent.
Market value of family labour, own seed and manure, and rent on own land.
Real figures are adjusted for inflation; nominal ones are not.
Kisan Credit Card, a revolving crop loan account.
Government pays part of the interest on short-term crop loans.

worked_example.title: Rebuild both income totals
worked_example.setup: Use the monthly figures per agricultural household in 2018-19.
steps: Cash-cost total, first part: 4,063 + 134 + 3,798 = 7,995.
Add animals and non-farm business: 7,995 + 1,582 + 641 = 10,218.
The gap between the two answers: 10,218 − 8,337 = 1,881.
Per person in an illustrative household of six: 10,218 ÷ 6 = 1,703.
worked_example.answer: ₹10,218 or ₹8,337 a month, a gap of ₹1,881; the first is about ₹1,700 per person for six people.

mistakes: Quoting ₹10,218 without saying that only paid-out costs were deducted.
Calling a household income figure a farmer's income, when it is per household and mixes in wages.
Reading a high average debt as proof of distress without asking who lent and what the loan paid for.
Treating the doubling target as met or missed without a later household survey.

recall.q: Why does the 77th round give two income answers?
recall.a: One deducts only paid-out expenses, the other also deducts imputed costs of family labour, own seed and own land.

recall.q: Which source of income overtook crops between 2012-13 and 2018-19?
recall.a: Wages, at 39.8 per cent of the total against 37.2 per cent for crops.

recall.q: What share of agricultural households had a loan in 2019?
recall.a: 50.2 per cent.

recall.q: Why is the average outstanding loan of ₹74,121 misleading for indebted households?
recall.a: It is averaged over all households, including the half with no debt.

recall.q: Name two questions to ask of any claim about farm incomes.
recall.a: Which survey and cost concept, and whether the figure is nominal or real.

sections.title: MSP, the CACP and procurement
sections.big_idea: MSP is an **offer to buy**, set above a cost, and which cost is used is the heart of the dispute.
in_plain_words: Each year the Union government announces MSPs for 22 mandated crops on the advice of the CACP. Public agencies stand ready to buy at that price where purchase centres operate. A private sale below MSP breaks no law.

Since 2018-19 the rule is a price at least 50 per cent above a cost of production. The margin printed beside each MSP rests on the cost column beside it. **Ask which cost concept is meant**, because C2 gives a smaller margin than a narrower cost. Few farmers sell to agencies, and buying is mostly rice and wheat.

diagram.caption: the path from advice to grain in the pool

key_terms.meaning: Minimum Support Price at which public agencies offer to buy a mandated crop.
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, which recommends MSPs.
A1 and A2 are paid-out costs; C2 and C3 add imputed costs.
Purchase of grain by the FCI and state agencies for the central pool.
Scheme that buys pulses, oilseeds and copra when prices fall below MSP.
Pays the gap between MSP and the market price.

worked_example.title: Check an MSP margin yourself
worked_example.setup: Take bajra in kharif 2026-27: MSP ₹2,900, cost used ₹1,858 a quintal.
steps: The 1.5 times rule gives a floor: 1,858 × 1.5 = 2,787.
The MSP of 2,900 is above that floor.
Margin over cost: 2,900 ÷ 1,858 = 1.56, which is 56%.
For wheat in the rabi 2027-28 announcement, the rise is 2,610 − 2,585 = 25 rupees.
As a share of the old price: 25 ÷ 2,585 = 0.97%.
worked_example.answer: Bajra's margin is 56%, and wheat's rise of ₹25 is 0.97%.

mistakes: Saying MSP is a legal floor on all trade. It is a price at which agencies offer to buy.
Reading a 106 per cent wheat margin as farmers doubling their money, when it depends on the cost concept.
Assuming most farmers sell at MSP, when 14.5 per cent of paddy households sold to an agency in 2019.
Ignoring stock build-up: open-ended buying raises storage and interest costs.

recall.q: How many crops have a mandated MSP?
recall.a: 22: 14 kharif, 6 rabi and 2 commercial. Sugarcane has a separate Fair and Remunerative Price.

recall.q: What did the Union Budget 2018-19 announce about MSP?
recall.a: That MSPs would be fixed at no less than 1.5 times the all-India weighted average cost of production.

recall.q: Which cost concept do farmers' movements insist on?
recall.a: The Swaminathan recommendation of 50 per cent above total cost, including family labour and rental value of owned land.

recall.q: What share of wheat output was sold at MSP in 2019?
recall.a: 20.8 per cent, down from 35 per cent in 2013.

recall.q: What does the Economic Survey propose over time?
recall.a: A move from physical procurement towards price-deficiency payments, bonuses and assured offtake.

sections.title: The 2020 farm laws and their repeal
sections.big_idea: Three laws came and went in **fourteen months**, and the argument they raised about MSP and state power is still open.
in_plain_words: The three Acts opened trade outside APMC yards, set up contract farming and eased stock limits. Together they would have created a second channel beside the mandis. The Supreme Court stayed them on 12 January 2021 and they were repealed on 30 November 2021.

Markets, land and agriculture are state subjects, so a central ban on state fees on outside trade reached into state territory. Supporters pointed to competition and lower costs. Critics feared for mandis, procurement and small farmers' bargaining power. **Judge each side's claim against the data** before you accept the slogan.

events.what: Repeal Bill passed by both Houses

key_terms.meaning: Agricultural Produce Market Committee that runs a regulated mandi.
Subjects where states legislate, including agriculture, land and markets.
A pre-sowing agreement between farmer and buyer, including the price.
A cap on how much of a commodity a trader may hold.
A vote with no recorded division.
The gap between MSP and the market price.

worked_example.title: Do most farmers depend on MSP?
worked_example.setup: Test the claim with the 2019 figures from the deck.
steps: Paddy households that sold to an agency: 14.5%.
So paddy households that did not: 100 − 14.5 = 85.5%.
Wheat households that sold to an agency: 9.7%, so 100 − 9.7 = 90.3% did not.
Add the structure: procurement stakes were highest where purchase centres are large.
worked_example.answer: The data does not support 'most farmers depend on MSP', though stakes were highest in procurement states.

mistakes: Saying the laws only affected Punjab and Haryana. The fee and trade provisions applied nationally.
Treating the repeal as the end of the MSP question.
Forgetting that a central law on market fees touches a subject the Constitution gives to the states.
Predicting effects from national averages without disaggregating by state and crop.

recall.q: Name the three Acts by what they did.
recall.a: Trade outside APMC yards, contract farming, and removal of routine stock limits on cereals, pulses, potatoes, onions and edible oils.

recall.q: When did the Supreme Court stay the laws?
recall.a: 12 January 2021.

recall.q: Which State List entry covers markets and fairs?
recall.a: Entry 28.

recall.q: What is the Goyal soybean study evidence for?
recall.a: Mandi prices rose after a private buyer's kiosks arrived, so competition and information can raise prices.

recall.q: What demand went beyond anything the Acts changed?
recall.a: A legal right to MSP and state procurement.

sections.title: The PDS and the National Food Security Act
sections.big_idea: The NFSA made subsidised grain a **legal entitlement**, and the same Act promises meals and a maternity benefit.
in_plain_words: The 2013 Act sets 5 kg per person a month for priority households, 35 kg for Antyodaya households, and coverage of 75 per cent of rural and 50 per cent of urban people. Section 13 names the eldest woman as head of the ration card.

Procurement and distribution are two ends of one system. MSP purchases fill the pool and the PDS draws on it. Delivery reforms trade two errors: grain reaching the wrong people and the right people missing out. **Count both**, as the Jharkhand biometric trial shows.

diagram.caption: one system from field to ration shop

key_terms.meaning: National Food Security Act 2013, a legal right to subsidised food.
A poorest household entitled to 35 kg a month.
Share of PDS grain that never reaches households.
Rice and wheat stock held for the PDS and buffer.
Makes the eldest woman aged 18 or over head of the household for the card.
One Nation One Ration Card, portability for migrants.

worked_example.title: Entitlement and leakage
worked_example.setup: An illustrative priority household has four people. The Schedule I price for rice is at most ₹3 a kg, and the Economic Survey says grain is now free.
steps: Monthly grain at 5 kg a person: 5 × 4 = 20 kg.
At the Schedule I rice ceiling: 20 × 3 = 60 rupees a month.
An Antyodaya household draws 35 kg instead of 20, a difference of 35 − 20 = 15 kg.
Leakage fell from 54 to 42 per cent in the NSS series: 54 − 42 = 12 percentage points.
worked_example.answer: 20 kg a month for the household; at most ₹60 at the ceiling price; leakage fell 12 percentage points.

mistakes: Treating the PDS as only a ration shop, when sections 4, 5 and 6 add meals and a maternity benefit.
Raising MSP or widening coverage without costing it on the other side of the food subsidy line.
Measuring only leakage and ignoring people wrongly cut off by a new verification step.
Assuming the 2011 Census coverage ceiling keeps pace with population.

recall.q: What coverage does section 3(2) set?
recall.a: Up to 75 per cent of the rural population and 50 per cent of the urban population.

recall.q: What did the Jharkhand biometric trial find?
recall.a: Less corruption, but 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point.

recall.q: Was NFSA coverage cut after the 2015 Shanta Kumar proposals?
recall.a: No. The committee proposed cutting coverage from 67 to 40 per cent, and coverage was not cut.

recall.q: What is the minimum maternity benefit under section 4?
recall.a: Not less than ₹6,000.

recall.q: What did Drèze and Khera find drove the fall in leakage?
recall.a: States that reformed their PDS, such as Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Bihar.

sections.title: Input subsidies: fertiliser, power and machinery
sections.big_idea: A price subsidy pays in proportion to use, so cheap urea and free power **reward the heaviest users** and distort the soil and the water table.
in_plain_words: Fertiliser and food subsidies dwarf every other farm programme. Urea is sold at a government price, so nitrogen is far cheaper than phosphorus and potassium, and the nutrient ratio has drifted from 4:3.2:1 to about 10.9:4.1:1. Monitoring improved control of flows without changing the price signal.

Free power works by rationing hours, which keeps average use in check but misallocates water. On small plots, hiring a machine for a day makes sense where owning one does not. **Soil health cards inform, but a price that rewards the wrong choice still wins.**

diagram.caption: each channel pays in proportion to use

key_terms.meaning: Government meets the gap between the retail price and the cost of supply.
Parts of nitrogen and phosphorus applied per part of potassium.
Pricing an input at its cost to the commons.
A centre where farmers hire machines by the day.
A record of soil test results for a farmer's plot.
Scheme for solar pumps and solarisation of farm power.

worked_example.title: Size the subsidy lines
worked_example.setup: Use the budget figures in ₹ crore from the deck.
steps: 2026-27 fertiliser subsidy against crop insurance: 1,70,781 ÷ 12,200 = 14.0 times.
2024-25 fertiliser subsidy against PM-KISAN: 1,70,683 ÷ 66,121 = 2.58 times.
2025-26 revised against budget for fertiliser: 1,86,460 − 1,67,887 = 18,573.
Nitrogen drift: 10.9 ÷ 4 = 2.73 times the 2009-10 ratio.
worked_example.answer: Fertiliser costs about 14 times the insurance line, the 2025-26 bill overshot by ₹18,573 crore, and the nitrogen ratio rose almost three-fold.

mistakes: Assuming more fertiliser gives the crop more nutrition when nutrients are out of balance.
Thinking a soil health card changes behaviour on its own.
Promoting solar pumps in an over-exploited block, where they remove the last cost of pumping.
Ignoring tenants when designing a per-acre transfer, since the owner may be paid while the tenant pays the higher urea price.

recall.q: Why does cheap urea cause overuse?
recall.a: It makes nitrogen far cheaper than other nutrients, so overuse is structurally embedded.

recall.q: What did Ryan and Sudarshan find in Rajasthan?
recall.a: Rationing keeps average water use near optimal but misallocates water across farmers.

recall.q: What does the Survey propose for urea?
recall.a: Raise the retail price modestly and transfer an equivalent amount per acre.

recall.q: What is the tenancy problem with that proposal?
recall.a: The transfer may go to the owner while the tenant pays the higher price.

recall.q: How many Custom Hiring Centres were set up by 2025-26?

sections.title: Irrigation and groundwater
sections.big_idea: India extracts about **61 per cent** of the groundwater it can replenish, but the north-west takes far more than it recharges.
in_plain_words: The irrigated share of cropped area rose from 41.7 to 55.8 per cent, with rice at about 67 per cent and millets under 15. Gross irrigated area counts a twice-irrigated hectare twice, so check whether a source reports gross or net.

The national stage of extraction is 60.63 per cent, yet Punjab is at 156.36. Free power, assured prices for paddy, a shared aquifer and weak enforcement all push towards pumping. **Water-saving technology can raise total use** if nothing limits extraction.

diagram.caption: stage of extraction, from worst to safest

key_terms.meaning: Annual groundwater use as a share of what can be extracted each year.
Gross irrigated area and gross cropped area.
A block taking out more water each year than is put back.
Water saved per hectare is used to irrigate more or thirstier crops.
PMKSY component paying 55 per cent of drip and sprinkler costs for small farmers.
A resource shared by users, where one's restraint helps the neighbour.

worked_example.title: Compute the stage of extraction
worked_example.setup: Use the 2025 assessment figures in billion cubic metres.
steps: Extraction over extractable resource: 247.22 ÷ 407.75 = 60.63%.
Share of units that are safe: 4,946 ÷ 6,762 = 73.14%.
Punjab at 156.36 per cent: 156.36 − 100 = 56.36 points above the sustainable level.
Delhi fell from 119.61 to 92.10 per cent: 119.61 − 92.10 = 27.51 points.
worked_example.answer: The national stage is 60.63%, 73.14% of units are safe, Punjab sits 56.36 points over the limit and Delhi improved by 27.51 points.

mistakes: Quoting the national 60.63 per cent as if every block were comfortable.
Reporting hectares under drip as if it showed less pumping.
Promoting a livelihood that needs new borewells in an over-exploited block.
Treating a block average as true for every well, from canal side to tail end.

recall.q: What is the national stage of extraction in 2025?
recall.a: 60.63 per cent.

recall.q: Which states extract above 100 per cent of what they can?
recall.a: Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana in the deck, at 156.36, 147.11 and 136.75 per cent.

recall.q: What is the rebound problem?
recall.a: Drip saves water per hectare but the farmer may irrigate more land or a thirstier crop, so total extraction holds or rises.

recall.q: Which crops are least irrigated?
recall.a: Millets at under 15 per cent and pulses at about 26 per cent.

recall.q: What should you look up before promoting a pump or crop?
recall.a: The category of the block you work in.

sections.title: Crop insurance and income support
sections.big_idea: PMFBY insures **yields by area** and PM-KISAN pays landholders a flat sum, so tenants and labourers are left out of one or both.
in_plain_words: PMFBY charges the farmer 2 per cent of the sum insured for kharif foodgrains, 1.5 for rabi and 5 for commercial crops. Governments pay the rest. Most claims settle on the average yield of a notified area, so a farmer whose own field failed may get nothing unless the loss is a localised peril.

PM-KISAN pays ₹6,000 in three instalments to landholding families with seeded records. It is small, regular and unconditional. **The quality of land records decides who receives it.** Evidence suggests it eases cash shortages for credit-constrained farmers.

key_terms.meaning: The amount of cover on which the premium is charged.
Paid from the estimated yield of the whole insurance unit.
A farmer with an active crop loan or KCC, enrolled automatically.
A sample harvest used to estimate yield for a unit.
Pays on a measured index such as rainfall.
Direct benefit transfer into a bank account.

worked_example.title: What does a farmer pay and receive?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative kharif foodgrain farmer insures ₹50,000 and receives the PM-KISAN transfer.
steps: Farmer premium at 2%: 50,000 × 0.02 = 1,000 rupees.
PM-KISAN per instalment: 6,000 ÷ 3 = 2,000 rupees.
Monthly equivalent: 6,000 ÷ 12 = 500 rupees.
Against the average agricultural household income of ₹10,218: 500 ÷ 10,218 = 4.9%.
worked_example.answer: The farmer pays ₹1,000 for the cover and receives ₹2,000 per instalment, about 4.9% of average monthly household income.

mistakes: Quoting 92.46 crore applications as if they were farmers.
Reading an enrolment trend without checking whether a state started or stopped paying the farmer premium.
Describing an association between beneficiary status and yields as a causal effect.
Forgetting that a woman is paid only if the land is in her name.

recall.q: What premium does a farmer pay for kharif foodgrains?
recall.a: 2 per cent of the sum insured.

recall.q: Why may a farmer with a failed plot get nothing?
recall.a: Claims are area-based, so the unit's estimated yield decides the payout unless the loss is localised.

recall.q: What did Cole and others find about index insurance demand?
recall.a: Only 5 to 10 per cent bought it, with price elasticity between -0.66 and -0.88; trust and liquidity mattered too.

recall.q: Who is excluded from PM-KISAN?
recall.a: Tenants, sharecroppers, landless labourers, income tax payers and government employees.

recall.q: Which PM-KISAN allocation figure should you quote?
recall.a: The budget document's ₹63,500 crore, noting the PIB gives ₹60,000 crore.

sections.title: Markets, extension and farmer producer organisations
sections.big_idea: Reform helps when farmers can see prices, choose a buyer and **bargain together**, and registration alone proves none of it.
in_plain_words: About half of households that grow paddy or wheat report a sale, while almost all soybean, cotton and sugarcane growers sell. A market reform therefore reaches cash-crop growers directly. e-NAM registers mandis, farmers and traders, but the test is the volume traded across mandis.

Goyal's soybean study found prices rose when kiosks gave information and a second buyer. Phone advice changed behaviour but not clearly yields. **An FPO that exists on paper still needs working capital, trusted grading and members free to sell.**

diagram.caption: four stages of an FPO and what to track

key_terms.meaning: National Agriculture Market, an electronic platform linking mandis.
Farmer Producer Organisation owned by its members.
Advice that helps farmers use seed, fertiliser and practices well.
Programme training input dealers in a 48-week diploma.
Pooling produce into larger lots that buyers will deal in.
Primary agricultural credit society.

worked_example.title: How many households actually sell?
worked_example.setup: Use the 77th round figures: share of agricultural households producing the crop, and share of producers reporting a sale.
steps: Paddy: 53.2 × 52.6 ÷ 100 = 28.0, so 28.0% of agricultural households report a paddy sale.
Wheat: 41.2 × 50.8 ÷ 100 = 20.9, so 20.9% report a wheat sale.
Compare scale: 58.02 lakh farmers trained by KVKs over three years.
worked_example.answer: About 28% of agricultural households sell paddy and 21% sell wheat; 47% of the 10,000 FPOs are on e-NAM.

mistakes: Treating registration on e-NAM as trade.
Assuming 10,000 registered FPOs means 10,000 working producer organisations.
Forgetting that a farmer who borrowed from a trader before sowing may be obliged to sell to him.
Reading a phone advice trial that found no yield gain as a failure, when it changed pesticide and crop choices.

recall.q: How many mandis were on e-NAM in June 2026?
What did Goyal's study find?
recall.a: Soybean mandi prices and acreage rose after a private buyer's kiosks gave price information and a second way to sell.

recall.q: What did the Avaaj Otalo trial find?
recall.a: Farmers relied less on neighbours and input sellers, used more effective pesticides and sowed more cumin, but no systematic yield or profit gain.

recall.q: Name two signs that an FPO was formed to meet a target.
recall.a: Members cannot say what it does for them; board and benefits concentrated in one group.

recall.q: Why does working capital matter?
recall.a: Without it the FPO cannot pay on delivery, so members sell to the trader who pays cash.

sections.title: Land records, tenancy and women in agriculture
sections.big_idea: Schemes pay the **recorded** owner, so tenants and many women who farm the land are invisible to them.
in_plain_words: PM-KISAN, the Price Support Scheme, PMFBY validation and any per-acre transfer all depend on land records. When a record is out of date, wrong or missing, the error passes into every scheme. A digital registry is only as accurate as the record it digitises.

Tenancy is a state subject. Fixed-rent, sharecropping and informal oral arrangements leave the tenant with no document. Women do much of the farm work: 76.9 per cent of rural women workers are in agriculture, but women are 13.96 per cent of holders. **Ask who the farmer on your list is.**

children.label: Tenant or sharecropper
items: In PMFBY with proof of tenure

children.label: Landless labourer
items: Reached by ration and work guarantee

key_terms.meaning: Tenant gives the owner a share of the harvest.
An oral agreement with no written lease.
Registry linking farmers to their plots.
Unpaid worker on a family farm in the survey.
Measures what people do in each half-hour of the day.
State List entry covering land tenures and landlord-tenant relations.

worked_example.title: Women among recipients and workers
worked_example.setup: Use PM-KISAN's 23rd instalment and the 2023-24 labour force figures.
steps: Women recipients: 2.18 ÷ 9.44 = 23% of those paid.
Gap between rural women and rural men in agriculture: 76.9 − 49.4 = 27.5 percentage points.
Unpaid time, women against men: 363 ÷ 123 = 2.95 times.
Compare holders: women are 13.96% of operational holders.
worked_example.answer: Women are about 23% of PM-KISAN recipients, work in agriculture 27.5 points more than men in rural areas, and spend nearly three times the unpaid time.

mistakes: Using 'farmer' to mean 'owner' when the programme pays by recorded title.
Scheduling training at midday or far from the village and expecting women to attend.
Assuming a yield gain from a new practice is free of extra unpaid female labour.
Writing off tenants as unreachable, when PMFBY has enrolled more than 1.44 crore with other proof of cultivation.

recall.q: Which scheme least depends on land and reaches the landless?
recall.a: The ration under the NFSA and the rural employment guarantee.

recall.q: What share of operational holders were women in 2015-16?
recall.a: 13.96 per cent.

recall.q: How does section 13 of the NFSA treat women?
recall.a: The eldest woman aged 18 or over is head of the household for the ration card.

recall.q: What proof can a tenant use for PMFBY?
recall.a: A tenure agreement or sowing certificate, as the state requires.

recall.q: Whom should you list in addition to the recorded owner?
recall.a: The person who cultivates.

sections.title: Climate risk, nutrition and food systems
sections.big_idea: Rain-fed crops face the biggest climate losses, and record harvests still sit beside **three in ten stunted children**.
in_plain_words: Model projections without adaptation show rain-fed rice losing 20 per cent of its yield by 2050 and wheat 19.3 per cent. Weather shocks already cut quality as well as quantity, and pulses suffer in El Niño years. The Odisha flood-tolerant rice trial shows that lowering the worst outcome raises investment.

Production and nutrition separate. Stunting fell from 35.5 to 29.3 per cent while wasting barely moved. **Farm policy sets what is cheap to grow and cheap to eat**, so diversification, millets in the PDS and natural farming are all food systems questions, each of which needs local evidence.

key_terms.meaning: ICAR network project that modelled climate effects on crops.
Low height for age in children under five.
Low weight for height in children.
Rice variety that survives submergence.
Lower risk encourages other investments.
Group of farmers organised under the National Mission on Natural Farming.

worked_example.title: Nutrition and natural farming numbers
worked_example.setup: Use NFHS-5, NFHS-6 and the natural farming figures.
steps: Fall in stunting: 35.5 − 29.3 = 6.2 percentage points.
Wasting barely moved: 19.3 − 19.0 = 0.3 points.
Natural farming clusters, 10.32 lakh hectares in millions: 10.32 ÷ 10 = 1.032 million.
Share of operated land: 1.032 ÷ 157.82 = 0.65%.
worked_example.answer: Stunting fell 6.2 points, wasting 0.3, and the clusters cover about 0.65% of operated land.

mistakes: Reading model projections as forecasts instead of comparisons under stated scenarios.
Judging a seed trial by yield alone and missing the extra area, inputs and credit.
Assuming record production means better diets.
Counting farmers enrolled in a natural farming programme without checking they still practise it.

recall.q: Which crop is among the most exposed to heat, per the deck?
recall.a: Wheat, a winter crop sensitive to heat at grain filling.

recall.q: What did the El Niño finding say about pulses?
recall.a: In 15 of 27 El Niño years pulse acreage fell 2 to 9 per cent and production 6 to 30 per cent.

recall.q: What did Swarna-Sub1 farmers do in addition to planting it?
recall.a: Used a more labour-intensive planting method, cultivated more area, used more fertiliser and took more credit.

recall.q: What share of children aged 6 to 23 months get an adequate diet?
recall.a: 15.3 per cent in NFHS-6.

recall.q: What are the first two steps for building climate risk into a programme?
recall.a: Exposure (rain-fed or irrigated) and water (the block's groundwater category).

sections.title: What evaluations have found, and sources
sections.big_idea: The evidence is **strong on information and buyer competition, descriptive on MSP and thin on the biggest schemes**.
in_plain_words: The course cites eight studies. Together they show what works at the margin: information and a second buyer raise prices, safer technology crowds in investment, delivery can improve quickly, and technology can both cut theft and cut people off.

The gap is as telling as the findings. Few rigorous evaluations cover the largest farm schemes, and the ministry study of PM-KISAN compares beneficiaries with others. **Where evidence is thin, say so** and design monitoring that can answer a causal question later. The ten questions at the end give you a way to start.

left.title: What we know
items: Information raises prices with a competing buyer

right.title: What we do not know well

key_terms.meaning: What would have happened without the scheme.
Participants differ from those who did not join.
A design comparing changes across groups and places.
An economic model estimated from data with geological variation.
Units are assigned to treatment by chance.
A link between two things that does not prove a cause.

worked_example.title: Match each claim to its evidence
worked_example.setup: A colleague gives you four claims. Decide which study design can support each.
steps: 'Insurance take-up is low because of price': a randomised trial varying price (Cole and others).
'Biometrics cut corruption': a randomised rollout across 132 sub-districts (Muralidharan and others).
'PM-KISAN raised wheat yields 1.93 per cent': a beneficiary comparison, so an association only.
'Rationing misallocates water': a structural model with geological variation (Ryan and Sudarshan).
worked_example.answer: Only the first, second and fourth rest on designs that address cause; the third is an association.

mistakes: Quoting a beneficiary-versus-non-beneficiary gap as the scheme's effect.
Assuming silence in the evidence means a scheme works.
Citing a figure without the date and source, when two official sources can disagree.
Copying a figure from a press release without opening the original document.

recall.q: What did Drèze and Khera find about PDS leakage?
recall.a: It fell from 54 to 42 per cent between 2004-05 and 2011-12 on NSS data, fastest in reforming states.

recall.q: How many farmers did PM-KISAN reach in the first three months in the IFPRI study?
recall.a: One third of farmers.

recall.q: What is the Economic Survey's idea on fertiliser, and its status?
recall.a: A price closer to cost plus an income transfer. It is a proposal for pilots and has not been tested at scale.

recall.q: Name two of the ten questions to ask of a scheme.
recall.a: Who is on the list, and whether the headline figure counts people, applications, hectares or rupees.

recall.q: What does the closing slide say to check before you design?
recall.a: The source, the unit and the list.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a route map. Twelve sections run from who farms, through incomes, prices, food, inputs and water, to risk, markets, land, climate and the evidence. If you work on one scheme, read section 1 first and then jump to the section that names it.
notes.4: Pick the source before you pick the number. The census counts **holdings**, the Situation Assessment Survey counts **agricultural households** and the labour force survey counts **workers**. Three units give three totals, and all three are right. Write the survey, the year and the unit beside every figure you copy.
notes.5: Read the table twice, once for holdings and once for area. Marginal holdings are 68.45 per cent of holdings and 24.03 per cent of land. Hold on to **86 per cent under two hectares**. A scheme sized for a farmer with several hectares reaches very few people.
notes.6: The average fell because the mix changed. Each class stayed near its own size, about 0.4 hectares for marginal holdings, while more holdings slid into that class as heirs divided the land. Read the trend as **more small holdings**, and the shrinking average as a side effect.
notes.7: Owner and operator are often different people. A tenant operates land and owns none, so a scheme that pays owners skips them. Before you design anything, **ask whether the list is built from ownership or operation**. Notice too why the NSS count of holdings, 101.98 million, sits below the census figure of 146.45 million.
notes.8: These are the households behind the word farmer. Note that **OBC households are 45.8 per cent** of agricultural households, and that Scheduled Castes are 15.9 per cent of them but 28.4 per cent of non-agricultural rural households. Cultivation was the main income source for 68.9 per cent of agricultural households in 2019.
notes.9: Work down the first table: seven in ten agricultural households hold under one hectare. Then compare caste shares of holdings with their shares of rural households. A scheme that pays per hectare owned will pay Scheduled Caste households **less than their numbers suggest**, because they run only 8.54 per cent of the area.
notes.10: Two facts here will date quickly. The 2021-22 census has finished fieldwork but is unpublished, so 2015-16 is still the latest. The 2025 labour force survey changed design, so its **43.0 per cent in agriculture** is not strictly comparable with earlier rounds. Always cite the year and carry the caution.
notes.11: Treat this as a glossary you come back to. The pair that trips people is **kharif and rabi**, the two crop seasons, plus the marketing season, which is the year a crop is sold. Keep three conversions handy: a lakh is 100,000, a crore is 10 million and a quintal is 100 kilograms.
notes.13: Income here is built from five lines: wages, rent from leased-out land, and net receipts from crops, animals and non-farm business. The survey gives two totals, ₹10,218 and ₹8,337. The gap is the cost of family labour and own land, so **pick the total that matches your question**.
notes.14: Wages now earn farm households more than crops do: 39.8 per cent of income against 37.2 per cent in 2018-19. Crop output rose over the period, so the fall in crop income points to **prices received and costs paid**. Check whether a figure is adjusted for inflation before you compare years.
notes.15: Value the family's own labour and the animal income nearly vanishes, from ₹1,582 to ₹441. That tells you it was mostly **unpaid family work**. Treat the ₹27 a day headline as a rough comparison, since it spreads crop income over a year. Ask for the distribution by land size.
notes.16: Debt is a rupee total that hides the terms. Half of households (50.2 per cent) owed something, and the average loan of ₹74,121 includes the half with none. Before reading distress into it, ask **who lent, at what rate and for what purpose**.
notes.17: Follow the four dates and you see the problem. A 2022 goal was set in 2016, yet the survey fielded in 2019 is the latest measure. Real income grew about 15 per cent in six years, so doubling looked very hard. **A target needs a named survey and a date** to measure it.
notes.18: Credit is a quiet channel here. The Kisan Credit Card gives a revolving crop loan, and interest subvention lowers the rate for those who repay on time. Notice that the Central region has 30 per cent of cropped area but **14.7 per cent of the subvention**. Then ask how tenants borrow without land records.
notes.19: Keep this slide as a checklist for any income claim. Name the survey, the cost concept, nominal or real, mean or median, household or person. The table pairs each common claim with its check. Try it: ₹10,218 for a household of six is about **₹1,700 a person**.
notes.21: MSP is an offer to buy. Agencies stand ready at that price, but a private sale below it is legal and buying happens only where centres operate. Remember the count: **22 mandated crops**, 14 kharif, 6 rabi and 2 commercial, with sugarcane priced separately as the Fair and Remunerative Price.
notes.22: Since 2018-19 the rule is an MSP at least 50 per cent above a cost. Check any row yourself by dividing MSP by cost. Paddy gives exactly 50 per cent and moong 61. The next slides show that **which cost is used** matters as much as the 50.
notes.23: Read the wheat line carefully. A ₹25 rise on ₹2,585 is the 0.97 per cent the slide reports. The 106 per cent margin looks generous, yet it **depends on the cost concept used**. You cannot conclude from it that wheat farmers double their money.
notes.24: This is the whole dispute on one slide. A1 and A2 count paid-out costs, C2 adds imputed family labour and owned land, and C3 adds management. Swaminathan's 50 per cent sits on the **full cost**. When someone says MSP is or is not 1.5 times cost, ask which cost they mean.
notes.25: Look at the bottom row. In 2019 only 20.8 per cent of wheat output and 23.7 per cent of paddy was sold at MSP, and wheat fell from 35 per cent in 2013. **MSP matters a great deal to a minority of farmers**, and it depends on where purchase centres stand.
notes.26: Procurement is big and concentrated. The 1,175 LMT headline is mostly rice and wheat, and pulses and oilseeds get far less. Remember the unit: **a lakh metric tonne is 100,000 tonnes**. The government's comparisons use periods of different length, so read them as the slide cautions.
notes.27: Read this as a trade-off. Buying everything offered at MSP guarantees a buyer but piles up stock, with storage and interest costs. The Survey proposes voluntary shifts and, in time, price-deficiency payments. The table lists each tool's **main risk**, which is what you should weigh in a design.
notes.29: Learn the three Acts by their job: one opened trade outside the mandi yards, one set up contract farming and one eased stock limits. Together they would have created a **second channel beside the APMC mandis**, free of the market fees the mandis charge.
notes.30: Memorise the order: pass, stay, announce, repeal. The Supreme Court stayed the laws on 12 January 2021, so they never fully operated, and repeal came on 30 November 2021. **Most of the argument ran outside Parliament**, at the protest sites and in the Supreme Court.
notes.31: Read this before you judge any market reform. Agriculture, water, land and markets are all state subjects, so a central law on market fees reaches into state territory. Six states passed resolutions against the Acts. **Any national reform has to work through state law.**
notes.32: Give the supporters their best case in four claims: more buyers, lower transaction costs, price certainty and private storage. Each is a hypothesis about behaviour. The soybean study from Madhya Pradesh backs the first one in a setting where a **private buyer competed with the mandi**.
notes.33: Now the critics' case: a fear for mandis and procurement, weak bargaining by marginal farmers, lost state revenue and a hurried process. One demand, a legal right to MSP, **went further than the Acts themselves**. Keep these strands apart when you hear someone summarise the protest.
notes.34: The repeal ended the laws and left the arguments. Use the table as a menu: each proposal has a champion and a cost. A legal guarantee needs either huge public purchase or a way to compel buyers. The Survey's idea is **a proposal that no national scheme yet implements**.
notes.35: Test the four claims against the data. Only 14.5 per cent of paddy and 9.7 per cent of wheat households sold to an agency, so 'most farmers depend on MSP' is hard to support. Then follow the closing prompts and **disaggregate by state and crop** before predicting any reform's effect.
notes.37: Memorise three numbers: 5 kg a person a month, 35 kg for an Antyodaya household, and coverage of 75 per cent rural and 50 per cent urban. Section 13 is the one people forget, since it puts **the ration card in the eldest woman's name**.
notes.38: Targeted PDS began in 1997 and the NFSA turned it into a legal right. The Survey says grain is now distributed free to eligible households. States identified 80.56 crore people against 81.35 crore intended, so they are **close to the ceiling**. Compare budget figures only within the same kind of estimate.
notes.39: Walk the five steps from mandi to ration shop. They explain why the state buys so much rice and wheat: the pool must be full for the PDS to draw on. The line to remember is **one budget line, two policies**. Raising MSP or widening coverage must be costed on both sides.
notes.40: Leakage is the gap between grain released and grain households say they bought, so the estimate depends on how you count. Drèze and Khera see 54 fall to 42 per cent, driven by reforming states like Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Bihar. Notice that **adding ad hoc allocations wrongly moved the figure** from 42 to 47.
notes.41: Remember this as the two-error rule. Biometric checks cut corruption in Jharkhand and also cut legitimate people off, 1.5 to 2 million at some point. The authors blame mainly **how the transition was managed**. Use the table to see which design choice trades one error for the other.
notes.42: The ceiling is a 2011 head count. As population grows the same 81.35 crore becomes a smaller share, and new families and migrants risk exclusion. The Shanta Kumar proposals of 2015, on coverage, cash and private procurement, **were not adopted**. Know both so you can place later debates.
notes.43: Look beyond the ration shop. The NFSA also gives pregnant women, lactating mothers and children anganwadi and school meals, plus a maternity benefit of at least ₹6,000. Use the table to find the **section number** for each channel whenever you cite the Act.
notes.45: Read across the rows for scale. Food and fertiliser are by far the largest lines, and the fertiliser line alone is more than two and a half times PM-KISAN. The 2025-26 revised fertiliser figure came ₹18,573 crore above budget, because **world prices drive the bill**.
notes.46: Urea is cheap at the counter, so farmers apply more of it. The Survey's key sentence says overuse is structurally embedded while one nutrient is vastly cheaper. Neem-coating and Aadhaar checks improved control of flows but **left the price signal unchanged**. Those who use most receive most subsidy.
notes.47: Read the chart as a drift away from balance. The nitrogen to potassium ratio went from 4 to about 10.9, while a typical benchmark sits near 4:2:1. The consequence is lower soil organic matter and plateauing yields. **The crop responds to balanced nutrients**, so more fertiliser alone does not help.
notes.48: Walk through the proposal: raise the urea price a little and pay an equal sum per acre. Efficient users keep their purchasing power and over-users have a reason to cut. The catch is tenancy. A per-acre payment to the owner leaves **the tenant paying more for urea**.
notes.49: Free power is rationed by hours, and Ryan and Sudarshan show the problem: average use is near the optimum but water goes to the wrong farmers. A high-value crop gets the same hours as a low-value one. Solar pumps, with near-zero cost per extra hour, can **deepen overpumping** in over-exploited blocks.
notes.50: Use this table as a screening tool. For each instrument ask who receives most and who is missed. Interest subvention misses informal borrowers and tenants, PM-KISAN misses tenants and labourers, and procurement misses districts with no centre. The deck says to **check the tendencies against your district's data**.
notes.51: Small plots make owning machines uneconomic, so hiring centres help, and 25,689 had been set up. Soil health cards show the same pattern: 26.09 crore issued while the nutrient ratio worsened. **Information alone cannot beat a price that rewards the wrong choice.**
notes.53: Memorise the contrasts. The irrigated share rose from 41.7 to 55.8 per cent, with rice at about 67, pulses about 26 and millets under 15. The crops the state wants more of are mostly rain-fed. Remember that **gross irrigated area counts a twice-irrigated hectare twice**.
notes.54: Learn the stage of extraction: use divided by what can be extracted each year, here 60.63 per cent. The category table shows most units are safe. The headline hides the 730 over-exploited units, so **look at the category counts** as well as the national average.
notes.55: The national average hides a concentrated problem. Punjab extracts 156.36 per cent of what it can, Rajasthan 147.11 and Haryana 136.75. A stage above 100 per cent means the aquifer is being mined. Delhi and Himachal show it can improve, so **read state and block figures**.
notes.56: The four forces reinforce one another: free power, assured prices for rice, a shared aquifer and weak enforcement. Note the commons logic, where one farmer's restraint benefits the neighbour. That is why advice to individuals needs **a collective rule behind it**.
notes.57: Programmes now aim at efficiency as well as area. Per Drop More Crop pays 55 per cent of drip and sprinkler costs for small and marginal farmers and 45 per cent for others. Treat the state examples as **reported outcomes**, since none is an independent evaluation.
notes.58: This is the rebound problem. Drip saves water per hectare, then the farmer irrigates more land or a thirstier crop, and total pumping holds or rises. Choose indicators that catch it, such as **water table depth and the block's stage of extraction**. Hectares under drip only record adoption.
notes.59: Use this as a field checklist. First find the block's category, then ask whether the livelihood needs new borewells, then pair any water-saving subsidy with a rule on total use. The sidebar warns that a **solar pump removes the last cost of pumping** in an over-exploited block.
notes.61: Scan the design table for the premium rates: 2 per cent for kharif foodgrains and oilseeds, 1.5 for rabi and 5 for commercial and horticultural crops. Most claims are **area-based**, so a farmer whose own field failed in a good unit may get nothing unless the loss is a localised peril.
notes.62: An application is one crop on one plot in one season, so 92.46 crore applications are far more than farmers. Quote them as applications. Compare claims of ₹2.06 lakh crore with the **total premium**, which includes the government share, before you judge the scheme's value.
notes.63: Enrolment moves with state decisions. When Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra paid the farmer's premium, enrolment rose very high and fell when they stopped. Andhra Pradesh went from 31.92 lakh to 7.43 lakh. The habit to build is to **check who pays the premium** before reading a trend.
notes.64: Notice the gap between worry and purchase. Households named rainfall as their top risk, yet only 5 to 10 per cent bought, and price elasticity was between -0.66 and -0.88. Price was only part of it. **Trust, cash at premium time and salience** matter too, so PMFBY deducts the premium from loans.
notes.65: PM-KISAN pays ₹6,000 a year in three ₹2,000 instalments to landholding families through Aadhaar-seeded accounts. Taxpayers and government employees are excluded. Notice the footnote: the PIB gives ₹60,000 crore for 2026-27 and the budget ₹63,500 crore. **Quote the budget document** and flag the gap.
notes.66: The transfer is flat per family, so per hectare it favours small holdings. It reaches landholders with updated records. Tenants, sharecroppers and labourers are outside by design. Use the table to classify any family you meet, and note that a woman receives it **only if the land is in her name**.
notes.67: Two studies, two strengths. The IFPRI study uses a triple difference with matching and finds help for credit-constrained farmers. The ministry-sponsored study compares beneficiaries with others, so its yield and income gaps are **associations only**. Ask what design sits behind any percentage you are handed.
notes.69: Check how much of a crop is sold at all. About half of paddy and wheat producers report a sale, while soybean, cotton and sugarcane growers almost all do, at 94 to 96 per cent. A market reform therefore touches cash-crop growers directly and subsistence grain growers **only at the margin**.
notes.70: e-NAM links mandis online, with ₹75 lakh per mandi for equipment. The registration counts, 1,656 mandis and 1.89 crore farmers, measure enrolment. The deck's test is **trade volume and the cross-mandi share**. Ask what share of a mandi's e-NAM trade is with buyers from outside it.
notes.71: Goyal's soybean study is the best evidence here for opening markets. Prices rose when kiosks gave price information and a second buyer arrived. The lesson is conditional, because it came from a setting where a **private buyer competed with the mandi**. Use the right-hand column as your local checklist.
notes.72: Extension reaches few farmers and input shops fill the gap. DAESI trains dealers over 48 weeks. Keep the scale in mind: 58.02 lakh farmers trained by KVKs over three years, against more than nine crore PM-KISAN families. **Reach is the weak point**, so ask who actually advises farmers in your area.
notes.73: Remember what the phone hotline did. Farmers called, relied less on neighbours and input sellers, changed pesticides and sowed more cumin. Yield and profit gains were not detected in a season with weather noise. **A study powered for adoption may miss yields**, so match your measures to your time frame.
notes.74: A registered FPO has a legal form, a board and a support agency. Whether it trades at scale and survives is a separate question. Of the 10,000 registered, 4,698 were on e-NAM. Use the four-stage table to **track outcomes beyond registration**.
notes.75: Treat this as a field checklist. Begin with one business, secure working capital and trusted grading, and plan for the end of support from year one. The failure table links each failure to an early sign. The one to remember: **members who owe a trader may not sell to the FPO**.
notes.77: Land records sit under almost every scheme here. PM-KISAN, the Price Support Scheme, PMFBY validation and a per-acre transfer all read them, so errors pass through. AgriStack builds a registry of farmers and plots. **A digital registry is only as accurate as the record it digitises.**
notes.78: Learn three tenure types: fixed rent, sharecropping and informal oral tenancy. The informal tenant holds no document to show a bank or insurer. The census counts such operators, yet schemes pay by recorded ownership. When a programme says farmers, ask whether it means **owners or cultivators**.
notes.79: Read the table by columns. The same tenant is in PMFBY with a tenure agreement or sowing certificate and out of PM-KISAN. The schemes least tied to land, the ration and the employment guarantee, **reach the landless**. Keep the table when you map who is covered.
notes.80: This tells you who works the land: 76.9 per cent of rural women workers are in agriculture against 49.4 per cent of rural men. A woman working daily on the family farm without wages is a helper in a household enterprise. Keep that in mind when you read the **10.8 per cent in regular wage jobs**.
notes.81: Set 64.4 per cent against 13.96 per cent. The first is women workers in agriculture, the second women among operational holders. Schemes that pay the recorded landholder mostly pay men. Recording land jointly would apply **the NFSA's ration card idea** to land.
notes.82: Care work and farm work stack up. On the survey day 41 per cent of women did caregiving against 21.4 per cent of men, and women spent 363 minutes on unpaid activities against 123. So **plan training around their day**, and expect a new practice to add to tasks women already do.
notes.83: Use the table as a design review. Each row asks a question and gives an answer: list the cultivator, pay into women's own accounts, hold training in the village with childcare, map tasks before and after adoption, open FPO membership without land title. Pick the **two rows your programme fails** and fix those first.
notes.85: The chart shows losses without adaptation. Rain-fed rice could lose 20 per cent by 2050, irrigated rice 3.5 and wheat 19.3. These are model projections, so use them for comparison. The pattern to remember: **irrigation buffers**, and wheat is exposed to heat at grain filling.
notes.86: Climate costs already show up in quality as well as quantity: iron, zinc and protein fall under high carbon dioxide and heat. Several large rice states yield below the national average. Pulses suffered in 15 of 27 El Niño years, so **rain-fed crops are hit first**.
notes.87: The trial's surprise lies in what farmers did with safer seed. Swarna-Sub1 lowered the worst outcome, so farmers planted more carefully, cultivated more area, used more fertiliser and took more credit. Learn to **measure area, inputs and credit** as well as yield.
notes.88: Hold the paradox: record production of grain, milk and horticulture alongside 29.3 per cent of children stunted. Stunting fell about six points but wasting barely moved, from 19.3 to 19.0. Production alone does not feed children. **Access, prices, diets, care, water and disease** decide the rest.
notes.89: This table links farm policy to the plate. MSP procurement favours rice and wheat, irrigation favours rice, imports shape oil and pulse prices, and millets in the PDS create demand. The last column states **likely effects**, so check them against local evidence.
notes.90: Compare scale. The 10.32 lakh hectares of natural farming clusters formed in 2025-26 are about 0.65 per cent of operated land. The Survey says organic and natural farming still cover a small fraction. Ask whether counted farmers **still practise it a season later**.
notes.91: Run the seven steps in order: exposure, water, hazards, varieties, insurance, diversification, nutrition. Each has a named evidence source, so you can fill the table from public data. Keep the Swarna-Sub1 lesson in mind: **lower the worst outcome** and investment rises.
notes.93: Read the evidence map as the limit of what this course can say. It lists eight studies with designs from randomised trials to a structural model. The footnote is the point: few rigorous evaluations cover the largest schemes. **Where evidence is thin, say so** and build monitoring that can answer causal questions later.
notes.94: Sort every market claim into what we know and what we do not know well. The evidence is strong on information and buyer competition, descriptive on MSP, and thin on e-markets and FPOs. Use the right-hand column of the table as a **list of research questions**.
notes.95: Two lessons for safety nets. PDS delivery can improve fast where states reform, and technology can cut theft or cut people off. PM-KISAN shows a small regular transfer eases cash constraints. The shared rule: **measure exclusion as carefully as leakage**, and keep a fallback.
notes.96: Three findings fit together: insurance demand is limited by price, trust and cash, safer technology crowds in investment, and free inputs get misallocated. Pair each finding with its implication in the table. The fertiliser proposal follows the same logic but **has not been tested at scale**.
notes.97: Make this a working list. Run the ten questions on one scheme in your district before your next planning meeting. Start with question 1, who is on the list, because the answers to the others depend on it. Then check whether the **headline counts people, applications, hectares or rupees**.
notes.98: These are the primary sources for the official numbers. When you cite a figure from this course, go to the original and check its date. Several are press releases or backgrounders from August 2026, so **record the date you accessed them** in your own notes.
notes.99: These are the studies behind the evidence sections. Use them to look up design details such as sample, setting and method. The closing line is a working rule: where two official sources disagree, as on the PM-KISAN allocation, **say so** in your own reports.
